title: The iPhone 18 Pro Is Almost Here. These Are The Rumors We Think Are Real
author: Jibin Joseph
content:
![](https://sm.pcmag.com/t/pcmag_uk/news/t/the-iphone/the-iphone-18-pro-is-almost-here-these-are-the-rumors-we-thi_c7ed.1920.jpg) (Credit: PCMag/Apple)
We're reportedly only a few weeks away from Apple's next iPhone event, which is likely to include the launch of a foldable, as well as iPhone 18 Pros.
Customers usually hold off on iPhone purchases right before Apple’s fall event, but the RAM crisis and its associated price hikes may have you wondering whether it's best to buy now and avoid any more increases. Apple already raised prices across several major product lines in June, but the iPhone was not included, helping drive iPhone 17 sales during the last quarter.
To make your decision easier, we’ve rounded up the biggest iPhone 18 Pro rumors we have heard so far. While these features and prices aren’t confirmed yet, they should help paint a picture of what to expect from Apple’s next big smartphones.
iPhone 18 Pro: Revised Lineup
The biggest rumor around the iPhone 18 lineup is its release timeline. Unlike previous years, where Apple released four phones in the same series in one go, Bloomberg reports Apple could take a two-pronged approach to ensure consistent revenue throughout the year.
Flagship phones, such as the iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and the first-ever foldable iPhone, could be unveiled in September, while the base iPhone 18, iPhone Air 2, and the iPhone 18e could be launched in spring 2027. We discuss the foldable iPhone in detail in a separate rumor round-up, so we’ll just stick to the Pro models here.
iPhone 18 Pro: Design and Colors
The iPhone 17 Pro models brought a major overhaul to Apple’s smartphone design language, with a new camera “plateau” and two-toned color scheme. This year, Apple isn’t expected to drastically change the device's appearance, but it could add a few bold colors and return to a more uniform color scheme on the back.
Several leakers, including Sonny Dickson and Instant Digital, claim that Apple could go with a never-before-seen cherry red and a new light blue, alongside the regular dark gray. Dickson also shared pictures of potential dummies, including one in light gray.
While the appearance of the rear is expected to remain the same, the in-hand feel could be a lot different. Ice Universe says the battery could get slightly larger on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, contributing to increased weight and bulk. More precisely, the leaker expects the device to be 0.25mm thicker and 7 grams heavier.
iPhone 18 Pro Display
On the front, we might see one significant change. The Dynamic Island, or the camera cutout, could be reduced by 35%, Ice Universe says. This won’t shrink the feature's overall functionality, but it could move the Face ID sensor’s illuminator to one corner below the screen.
When it comes to display sizes, the consensus is that the iPhone 18 Pro will come in its usual 6.3-inch screen, while the Pro Max will have a 6.9-inch screen. Apple, however, has reportedly been pushing suppliers to provide much brighter displays and could use the more power-efficient LTPO+ display tech.
iPhone 18 Pro Cameras
The iPhone 17 Pro lineup bumped all three cameras to 48MP. For the iPhone 18 Pro, the biggest camera-related rumor we have heard is around variable aperture. While the iPhone 17 models had a fixed aperture, the iPhone 18 Pro may introduce a variable aperture. ETNews reports that the modified system has already entered production and would help the cameras deliver more light to the sensors in dark conditions and reduce light in bright conditions.
Apple may also modify its relatively new Camera Control button. Introduced with the iPhone 16, the capacitive button at the bottom right of the phone lets you quickly launch the Camera app, take pictures, and adjust settings for zoom, exposure, depth, and other controls. Mastering the capacitive button, however, has proved difficult, with users noting that they have been accidentally launching the Camera app. Apple may finally fix the problem by removing the touch-sensitive components of the button and delivering a more user-friendly experience, 9to5Mac reports.
iPhone 18 Pro Performance
The iPhone 18 Pro is likely to receive a performance boost with the A20 chip. It will use TSMC’s 2nm technology, an upgrade from the previous generation’s 3nm tech. The transition will allow more transistors on each chip but also raise chip costs by 50%, MacRumors reports.
The chip is also rumored to have TSMC’s Wafer-Level Multi-Chip Module (WMCM) technology, which infuses RAM into the same wafer as the CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine. Overall, it is expected to be 18% faster and 30% more power-efficient than than previous generations, according to leaker Fixed Focus Digital.
Apple usually reserves the base variant of its chip series for the standard iPhone models, while the Pro models get the corresponding Pro chip. With the iPhone 18 series, Apple is reportedly considering offering just the high-end variant across the lineup.
Another expected upgrade is for the modem. The iPhone 17 Pro models had an unspecified third-party modem, but the iPhone 18 Pro could get the company’s proprietary C2 modem. It will support 5G satellite connectivity and reduce the scope of location data retained by networks, according to MacRumors.
iPhone 18 Pro Battery
Apple never reveals its battery capacities, but multiple leakers have indicated a larger and more efficient battery for the iPhone 18 Pro Max. According to Digital Chat Station, the top variant will have a capacity of up to 5,200mAh, slightly better than the 5,088mAh capacity of its predecessor. With a more efficient modem and processor, the battery life could be significantly longer. The iPhone 18 Pro, on the other hand, could see a minimal bump from 4,252mAh to 4,288mAh.
More recently, leaks posted on Korean and Chinese social media sites tip a US iPhone 18 Pro Max model with a 5,567mAh battery, a nearly 10% increase over the iPhone 17 Pro Max, MacRumors notes.
iPhone 18 Pro: Pricing and Release
This is what much of the decision-making hinges on. Apple has avoided raising prices for its biggest revenue generator, but rising RAM and storage costs are unavoidable, by outgoing CEO Tim Cook’s own admission.
Common sense suggests a price hike for iPhones is inevitable in September. According to The Wall Street Journal's estimate, rising component costs would push the iPhone 18 Pro to start at $1,299. If you couple that with recent Apple trends, the iPhone 18 Pro Max could be priced $100 higher, taking its starting price to $1,399. In comparison, the iPhone 17 Pro starts at $1,099, while the 17 Pro Max starts at $1,199.
When asked on a recent earnings call about potential price hikes for the iPhone, Cook said it's "too early to come to a definitive conclusion of what happens there. Because it takes a little while for the channels to adjust since there's channel inventory, it takes a while for the consumer to respond. We'll understand that more in the weeks ahead."
The iPhone 18 Pro’s release date hasn’t been finalized yet. Going by previous event dates, Sept. 9, 2026, probably makes the most sense for the announcement, with a ship date the following week, but we'll have to wait for those invitations to hit our inboxes to know for sure.
summary: Apple's upcoming iPhone 18 Pro lineup is rumored to feature a split release schedule, new design colors, and a potential variable aperture camera system. Performance is expected to improve with a new A20 chip utilizing 2nm technology and a proprietary C2 modem. However, rising component costs may lead to higher starting prices of $1,299 for the iPhone 18 Pro and $1,399 for the Pro Max.
key_points: Apple may split the iPhone 18 release, launching Pro and foldable models in September and base models in spring 2027.
The Dynamic Island cutout could shrink by 35%, and the iPhone 18 Pro may introduce a variable aperture camera system.
Performance is expected to be boosted by a new A20 chip built on TSMC's 2nm technology.
Rising component and RAM costs are expected to drive starting prices up to $1,299 for the Pro and $1,399 for the Pro Max.

title: Gears of War: E-Day and Gibson Unite for a Custom Guitar Collection
author: Danielle Partis; XBOX Wire Editor
content:
As we count down to the launch of Gears of War: E-Day, Gibson Guitars and The Coalition are teaming up with a one-of-a-kind collaboration that brings together two legendary brands built on craftsmanship, authenticity, and storytelling.
The collaboration is a natural extension of Gears’ musical identity. Guitar-driven scores have helped define the franchise for nearly two decades, and Gears of War: E-Day composer Adam Lastiwka used Gibson guitars in the recording of the game’s soundtrack.
Inspired by the enduring brotherhood at the heart of Gears, the collection features two custom Gibson guitars based on the iconic Les Paul and SG designs. Created exclusively for Gears of War: E-Day, the guitars honor franchise heroes Marcus Fenix and Dominic Santiago through striking original artwork from acclaimed artist and illustrator Luke Preece.
“These guitars feel like the culmination of a years-long creative collaboration with Luke, who has been part of Gears of War: E-Day from the very beginning,” says Studio Brand Director Nicole Fawcette. “He loves Gears of War as much as we do, and he has a gift for translating the spirit of the franchise into striking art that makes you feel something.”
For artist Luke Preece, the project was a natural fit. “It brought together everything I love – music, metal, guitars, video games, art, and Gears of War,” he says. “All of those influences found their way into the guitars, so the collaboration felt completely natural.”
That sense of shared creative direction shaped the collaboration from the start. “Nicole and I had already established the visual language for E-Day, and we had a clear plan,” Preece adds. “We work well together and are usually on the same page, which gave us the freedom to focus on making the designs as strong as possible.”
![](https://xboxwire.thesourcemediaassets.com/sites/2/2026/08/Gears-Gibson-Spare-inline-164d65160610516cac79-1024x576.jpg)
Crafted for Brotherhood
Each guitar began as a hand-drawn concept before being digitally mapped, carefully stenciled, and meticulously hand-painted by Preece. Every detail was designed to capture the spirit of Gears through the lens of two of its most beloved characters.
The collection draws inspiration from two of the games “Emotional Core” pillars, Brutality and Pathos, ideas that reflect both the grit and sacrifice woven throughout the story of Gears of War: E-Day.
“What I love most about Luke’s work is his ability to communicate big, loud, bold ideas,” Fawcette says. “Rather than simply illustrating Marcus and Dom, we had the opportunity to distill their themes and energy into something iconic.”
![](https://xboxwire.thesourcemediaassets.com/sites/2/2026/08/Gears-Gibson-Marcus-LP-4d70589545554c8a51bd-1024x576.jpg)
Marcus Fenix | Brutality
Represented on Gibson’s legendary Les Paul, Marcus’ guitar embodies the grit, determination, and relentless spirit that have defined the character for nearly two decades.
At the center sits a weathered skull against a COG Tag backdrop, framed by the unmistakable blades of a chainsaw. Splashes of Locust blood and fractured textures evoke the chaos of Emergence Day and the world-shattering events that changed Sera forever. The result is a bold, aggressive design that celebrates one of gaming’s most iconic heroes while paying tribute to the franchise’s signature imagery.
“Marcus’ Les Paul was the hardest to solve. The hardware interrupted some of the original ideas, so we leaned into the circular saw-blade motif. It gave the piece the aggressive, brutal energy we wanted, and the shape fit the body of the guitar perfectly,” says Preece.
![](https://xboxwire.thesourcemediaassets.com/sites/2/2026/08/Gears-Gibson-Dom-SG-4fc8981bb05df225bb8c-1024x576.jpg)
Dominic Santiago | Pathos
Dominic Santiago’s design finds its home on the equally iconic Gibson SG, delivering a more somber and reflective counterpart.
A tearful, battle-worn skull stands against a COG Tag surrounded by barbed wire and vibrant crimson poppies, a powerful symbol of remembrance woven throughout Gears lore. The artwork reflects Dom’s unwavering loyalty, personal sacrifice, and the emotional weight carried by one of the franchise’s most beloved characters.
“Dom’s design came together more naturally through its symbolism,” says Preece. “The wings flowed beautifully with the shape of the SG and connected with the pathos of his story, including the angelic imagery associated with Maria.”
Together, the guitars tell a story of brotherhood, resilience, loss, and fate, themes that remain central to the world of Gears of War.
“Early on, we considered physically distressing the guitars to make them feel battle-worn,” says Fawcette. “In the end, I’m glad we preserved the beauty of the instruments and allowed the artwork itself to carry the weight and intensity.”
See the Guitars at Gamescom
“We can’t wait for fans to see these in-person,” says Fawcette. “Each guitar is already a beautiful object, and Luke’s hand-painted Gears artwork transforms it into something visually stunning – a genuine work of art that feels cool, heavy, and unmistakably Gears.”
Fans attending Gamescom 2026 in Cologne, Germany will be among the first to see the collection in person when they make their public debut at the XBOX booth.
Says Preece, “Only four guitars were made. Each is numbered and signed, and because they were painted by hand, even the repeated designs are not exact copies. Every instrument is a unique, one-of-one piece.”
Win a Piece of the Brotherhood
Starting today, fans can enter for a chance to win three custom guitars in total: two Marcus Fenix-inspired Les Pauls and one Dominic Santiago-inspired SG.
Fans in official XBOX supported regions can enter the giveaway starting today by leaving a comment tagging your Gears of War: E-Day companions and using #GearsofWarGibsonSweepstakes on the announcement post hosted on the @gibsonguitar and @gearsofwar Instagram accounts, for a chance to win one of the three guitars. The winners will be selected at random and announced on October 16, 2026. Check out the full rules, terms and conditions here.
Whether you’re a lifelong Gears fan, a collector of iconic instruments, or appreciate exceptional craftsmanship, the collaboration between Gibson and Gears of War: E-Day offers a rare opportunity to own a piece of Gears of War history as we prepare for Emergence Day.
Gears of War: E-Day launches October 6, 2026, on Xbox Series X|S, Xbox PC, Steam, and is available day one with Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass.
summary: Gibson Guitars and The Coalition have partnered to create a limited-edition collection of custom guitars inspired by Gears of War: E-Day. Artist Luke Preece hand-painted four unique instruments honoring franchise heroes Marcus Fenix and Dominic Santiago. Fans attending Gamescom 2026 can view the guitars, and a sweepstakes is being held to give away three of the instruments.
key_points: Composer Adam Lastiwka used Gibson guitars to record the soundtrack for Gears of War: E-Day.
The collection features two custom designs: a Marcus Fenix Les Paul representing brutality and a Dominic Santiago SG representing pathos.
Only four hand-painted, signed, and numbered guitars were created by artist Luke Preece.
Fans in supported regions can enter a giveaway on Instagram to win one of three custom guitars until winners are announced on October 16, 2026.
Gears of War: E-Day launches on October 6, 2026.

title: 'Subnautica Began With a Love for the Ocean' — Subnautica 2 Dev Makes $100,000 Donation to Ocean Cleanup Charity as It Releases 1.2 Patch
author: Wesley Yin-Poole
content:
Subnautica 2 Early Access 1.2 is out now, adding the Buddy System to the underwater survival and crafting game.
Developer Unknown Worlds has also announced a $100,000 donation to the appropriately named ocean cleanup non-profit The Ocean Cleanup.
Unknown Worlds previously donated a portion of proceeds from the original Subnautica to The Ocean Cleanup on World Environment Day in 2019, and has continued to support ocean conservation efforts since.
“Subnautica began with a love for the ocean, and it means a great deal to continue the conservation work we started with the original game through this donation to The Ocean Cleanup,” said executive producer Fernando Melo. “We will keep doing our part to protect the ocean we have spent so long bringing to life.”
Unknown Worlds spoke about what to expect from Subnautica 1.2 yesterday, but today's release of the update brings with it detailed patch notes, below, which include a long list of changes and fixes.
1.2 includes the first iteration of Subnautica 2 proximity chat via an in-game voice chat option that you can use with your friends to talk locally with each other. As you get farther away it will switch to a radio-sounding voice that will progressively break up to a point where you can almost not hear your friend.
Also added is player emotes via a small menu that lets players cheer on their friends, clap, or tell them you’re a little annoyed or frustrated. Inventory sharing lets players walk up to another player, access their inventory and quickly swap items between one another, rather than having to drop inventory items out in the world and have them pick them up. Player revives are also added, so if your friend is downed for whatever reason, you’ll have some time to share some oxygen with them and bring them back to life.
Two additional player characters (Grace and Jegna) are added alongside two new suit colors. Also included is the tracking tag, a short-range beacon you can throw out in the environment or put inside an inventory such as a portable locker, so if you ever leave it in a cave you can find your way back to it. If you die holding a tracking tag or have one in your inventory, it will extend your black box signal to help you find the stuff you left behind.
Improved HUD icons means all the icons will not be at full scale by default, but when you mouse over them after a half second or so they will scale up and give you the full details. Alongside that, there are improved pinned recipes, which means the UI should feel a little less confusing, and improvements to the base builder tool that should help make it clearer when you can and can't build something.
The Subnautica 2 Early Access 1.2 update patch notes, courtesy of Steam, are below:
Subnautica 2 Early Access 1.2 patch notes
Gameplay
- 🤿Added Cross-Platform Voice Chat. Multiplayer host can choose between Global and Proximity Voice Chat (as players get further away, they become harder to hear). Voice Chat is available as “always on,” “push to talk,” or “always off.”
- Tracking Tag added to the game. Can be placed in carryables (like a locker) as a short-range beacon. If present in hand or inventory when reprinting, will increase black box range.
- Players can now revive each other before reprinting. Revived players will keep their equipment and regain a small amount of oxygen. Downed players can also choose to immediately reprint and respawn back at their assigned Biobed.
- Added Wave, Clap, Thumbs Up, Thumbs Down, and Frustrated emotes. Emotes are selectable from a new radial menu. Triggerable in water or on land, and can be interrupted by gameplay input.
- 🤿Players can now interact with each other to directly exchange inventory items.
- Added Jegna and Grace character options in Character Customization, as well as two new color schemes for characters.
- Interaction text on Upgrade Biobeds changed to clarify their use.
- Added a distinct beep to player upgrade spots within a small radius.
- Added a small flash to screen on Upgrade Biobeds.
Fauna & Flora
- Added flinch animations and VFX to Marrowbreach, Hammerhead, Nibbler, Needlershark, Epicurean, and Twin Eel.
- Adjusted Bulletheads so they deal more damage but can now be dodged (...sometimes).
- Added more Coral Crab animations.
- Revised model and animations for the Bloom Parasite.
- Improved Jelly Ring tentacles.
Resources
- More Carryable Racks added to early game wrecks and human-made sites.
Base Building
- 🤿Improvements made to the base building system’s placement UI, including alignment guide lines.
- Improvements made to how the game handles Move mode for clients in a multiplayer session.
- Updated Tadpole Dock icon to reflect updated model.
- Base edits now account for size snapping, such that it’s possible to fully deconstruct a room with Shrink (among other things).
- Trashcan is now functional as a trashcan. Items added to trashcan will be destroyed one by one after a short, five second delay.
- Bases can no longer be built inside of Great Jaw.
- Items that are preventing an object from being built are displayed in a list.
Vehicles, Tools & Equipment
- Changed Feedback Resonator’s interaction with creatures to stun them instead of causing them to flee.
- Extended duration of the Sonic Resonator creature stun to 10 seconds.
- Sources for Acid now appear as green dots in the Scanner HUD.
- Repair Tool now unlocks after two scans.
- Tadpoles that are destroyed outside of the Early Access fence teleport inside of the Early Access fence so that they can be recovered.
Menus & UI
- Signals adjusted to increase clarity and reduce HUD clutter. Icons get larger as player gets closer, and text will appear on hover for signals further away.
- Save Codes can now be directly pasted into the Cloud Save Download input box.
- Builder menu’s scroll position persists when closing and re-opening the menu.
- Pinned recipes highlight when the player acquires resources relevant to those recipes.
- Items shown in Pinned Recipes are no longer dimmed, to improve readability.
- Improved error language for errors specific to non-Game Pass Microsoft users.
- Audiologs show elapsed and remaining playback time.
Art & Visual FX
- VFX performance improvements to the Graveyard and its Water Slugs, for the players who collect hundreds of Water Slugs.
- Tallshrooms now have an icon in the Scanner HUD.
- Added impact VFX for Tongue Thief.
- Light poles connecting Observatory and Rosetta Stone added.
- Removed odd blue outline that was sometimes visible on Collector Leviathan.
- Improved consistency of sparks VFX across the game.
- Improved consistency of electricity VFX across the game.
- Added shock VFX for Hammerheads impacting objects.
- Added more environmental effects to abandoned outposts and wrecks.
Voice & Narrative
- Previously unlocalized lines are now localized.
- Naming of Carryable Racks is now consistent across the game, instead of sometimes being “Wall Rack” or “Hardpoint.”
- Reduced frequency of NOA alerts.
- Adjusted Welcome Center message in Spanish and Italian.
- Adjusted pacing of dialog to better match the actions occurring during the recordings.
- Added Databank entry for Mod Station.
- Added Databank entries for audiologs that were missing them.
- Further refinements to voice over prioritization, so the most important lines are heard.
Music & SFX
- Music added to Tufa Zona, Thermal Area, and North Coral Gardens.
Miscellaneous
- New Privacy Policy additions from July 15th will pop up on first play.
- New Frame Generation modes 5x and 6x (RTX 5000 series) added.
- New Dynamic Frame Generation added. Will automatically select the appropriate Frame Generation mode to get a good performance (RTX 5000 series).
- VSync and DLSS Frame Generation can be turned on at the same time.
- Added description for Nvidia Reflex in Settings.
- Reorganized order of volume sliders.
- The in-game Feedback Tool now allows attaching a save file.
Bug Fixes
- Fixed Collector Leviathan performing a 360 spin whenever it grabs or throws a Tadpole.
- Fixed an issue where settings menus would sometimes become cut-off while navigating with controller/gamepad.
- 🤿Fixed an exploit where swapping the resource in an occupied Metal Farm caused the new resource to inherit the growth time of the previous resource.
- 🤿Fixed an issue where opened Angel Combs’ cankers could incorrectly appear closed after a game update.
- Pausing the game while sprinting no longer causes the player to permanently sprint.
- Fixed some Axum/Tailings furniture being buildable outside of the player’s base, which caused multiple knock-on problems.
- Tadpole can no longer be docked when there is insufficient space for it, resolving an issue where the Tadpole could become stuck in its dock.
- 🤿Additional fixes to the tool prompts to account for accuracy and recipe-sharing between players in a multiplayer session.
- Fixed Power Transmitter ray visibility and overall appearance, particularly for multiplayer clients who alternately saw extra rays or had rays that should be there disappear.
- 🤿Fixed Hydroturbines stopping their power production after 120-160 mins of gameplay, after the player swam away from them, and for their turbines to stop spinning, even when producing power.
- Fixed music playing in the incorrect region or not playing at all in intended areas.

- Fixed an issue where pressing the spacebar during the TOS skipped the step of agreeing to it.

- Fixed an issue where chassis signals could remain visible on screen even when the chassis is equipped to the Tadpole.
- Fixed the player’s dive mask clipping into the camera while adjusting FOV in the Settings menu.
- 🤿Fixed several terrain, resource, and world object clipping, floating, gap, extended collision, misplacement, and texture issues.

- Fixed Jetocaris’s PDA image not matching the in-game creature model.

- Fixed an issue where using Unstuck while holding a carryable Utility would prevent players from being able to pick up other Utilities or equip hotbar items.
- Added corrections to the scannable highlight for objects that were missing it.

title: Google Pixel 11 Pro Review: One Small Step for Phones
author: Chris Niccolls
content:
Gone are the days of major technological and hardware upgrades from model to model, at least when it comes to the digital camera industry. Smartphones are no exception, and it seems that any annual changes we do see tend to be relatively minor now.
I feel like the Pixel 11 Pro series provides plenty of customization and control of my images if I want to be more hands-on, but is still simple enough to be usable for casual users to enjoy.
Pros
- Better telephoto camera and processor
- Generative AI is less in-your-face
- The color "Looks" are fun to use and very customizable
- Magic Capture is a useful feature with minimal fluff
- Many features and functions are much faster
Cons
- Battery life is virtually the same as last year
- The Pixel fully supports Nano Banana AI but using it through Gemini is convoluted
- Image quality improvements are largely incremental
As part of its yearly release cycle, Google has announced the Pixel 11 series of phones, and with the new Pixel 11 Pro XL in hand, I proceeded to test this latest model, not as a phone, but rather as a creative photographic tool. Sadly, the current memory crisis has inflated costs across the industry, and the Pixel 11 Pro XL is going to run you at least $1,299.
![A close-up, angled view of the back of a light gray smartphone featuring a prominent, horizontal, pill-shaped camera module with three lenses and a flash, and a white "G" logo centered on the body.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/Pixel-11-Pro-XL-0006-800x533.jpg)
Google Pixel 11 Pro XL Review: How It Feels
Both the Pro and Pro XL phones run the same cameras and have the same options for storage and RAM. However, the XL version that I tested comes with a brand-new 6.8-inch screen that now peaks at a maximum of 3,600 nits of brightness. The body design is quite similar to last year’s, comes in four colors, and features a new camera bar design. External controls are, otherwise, almost identical to the 10 series. The weight hovers around eight ounces (226 grams), which does bring it down ever so slightly from last year’s model.
![A white smartphone with a prominent, pill-shaped camera module on the back lies on a light green, marbled surface.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/Pixel-11-Pro-XL-0005-800x533.jpg)
![Two light blue smartphones stand side-by-side against a black background, labeled "Pixel 10 Pro XL" and "Pixel 11 Pro XL" respectively.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-vs-10-800x450.jpg)
The internal battery has also dropped slightly to a maximum of 5,115 mAh. In exchange, the Pixel 11 Pro XL features a more efficient main camera sensor and the new G6 Tensor processor, which reduces power demands. I’d say that overall power usage and longevity will be similar to what we had before, which is always disappointing when talking about battery life. It’s unclear why the battery got smaller.
We also see the return of the Google Pixel Snap magnetic attachment system, which works with MagSafe accessories and chargers. Wired charging is still around 45 watts, but the wireless charging speeds have been improved this time around.
![A smartphone screen displays a "Hi there" welcome message on a black background, resting on a light green marble surface.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/Pixel-11-Pro-XL-0001-800x533.jpg)
![A silver smartphone with a prominent horizontal camera bar on its back stands upright against a pale green marble background.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/Pixel-11-Pro-XL-0008-800x533.jpg)
Google Pixel 11 Pro XL Review: The Cameras
The ultra-wide camera returns from the last model with the same 48-megapixel Type 1/2.51 sensor and f/1.7 aperture. The main camera is also very similar, though as mentioned above, it is a more power-efficient design. It features a 50-megapixel Type 1/1.3 sensor, has a fixed f/1.68 aperture, and the image quality is very similar to what we have seen before.
![A close-up of a smartphone camera module next to text listing specifications: 48MP Quad Bayer, 12mm Equivalent FOV, f/1.7, and Type 1/2.51.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Ultrawide-800x450.jpg)
![A young girl in a baseball cap and Crocs stands on rocks by a river at sunset, holding a fly fishing rod.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/PXL_20260818_023611435.RAW-01.COVER_-601x800.jpg)
![A close-up of a camera lens with text below it reading: 50MP Quad Bayer, 24mm Equivalent FOV, f/1.68, Type 1/1.3.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Main-Camera-Fixed-800x450.jpg)
![A reflection of vibrant red autumn leaves and dark tree branches appears on the rippled, murky surface of a puddle.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/PXL_20260813_193213707.RAW-01.COVER-LOOKS-STANDARD-VANILLA-601x800.jpg)
The selfie camera is the same 42-megapixel f/2.2 camera as before.
The only major hardware change is with the telephoto camera, which gives a 5x zoom equivalent and is now mated to a larger Type 1/1.95 sensor. You still get an f/2.8 aperture on the lens and optical image stabilization to help capture the shot, too. I noticed a distinct improvement in low-light image quality as well as better overall detail reproduction. It’s always nice to see real hardware changes, and the new telephoto lens is a meaningful improvement.
![A young girl with long red hair and freckles looks toward the camera while holding a menu in a restaurant.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/PXL_20260813_224103239.PORTRAIT-PIXEL-11-PRO-Portrait-mode-Classic-601x800.jpg)
![Two side-by-side images show a wooden box labeled with Japanese calligraphy resting on a shelf above a set of patterned blue and white ceramic bowls.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Telephoto-Comparison-800x450.jpg)
The phone can push beyond to a digital 30x zoom equivalent, but the image quality is noticeably cropped. However, Google has also increased the Pro Zoom AI-generated 100x range to a further 120x range now. This technology takes the woefully poor resolution of a 120x zoom crop and digitally enhances it using generative AI. Beyond the ethical questions, the result is actually usable, especially if the final output is just social media. However, the generative enhancement can only effectively be applied to non-human subjects, and any text will be guessed at with nonsense shapes if the source writing is too small or otherwise undecipherable. An extra 20x zoom at this already far reach is an incredibly minor improvement, regardless of how you feel about the technology.
![The rear corner of a dark-colored sedan is parked next to a white fence post and stone wall.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/PXL_20260813_021555963.BURST-01.COVER-Pixel-11-PRO-RES-120X-601x800.jpg)
![A side-by-side comparison of a dog in tall grass, showing a blurry "Before Processing" image on the left and a sharper, clearer "After Processing" image on the right.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-120x-Pro-Zoom-800x450.jpg)
Google Pixel 11 Pro XL Review: How It Shoots
If there isn’t much to talk about with hardware improvements, then that is because Google instead chose to make changes to the software this time around. The first one to tackle is the Magic Capture mode.
Effectively, Magic Capture works by allowing the user to record a memory or moment in video and then lets the phone pick out ideal images to document the event as stills. The Pixel will largely decide this based on faces looking at the camera and smiling, interesting colors and backgrounds, as well as moments of action. Think of it like an extended pre-capture mode on a mirrorless camera, except you don’t get every photo and you don’t decide which ones to keep, at least not initially.
![A young girl with long reddish-brown hair sits on a patio chair while a curly, light-brown dog stands on its hind legs to greet her.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Pulling-Frames-800x450.jpg)
![A young girl with long red hair sits in a patterned outdoor chair, smiling while holding a curly, light-brown dog in her lap.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/PXL_20260817_165335632.MC_-601x800.jpg)
You end up with a 1080p resolution video that you can use as you see fit and a series of high-quality 12-megapixel images from key moments throughout that clip. You can scrub through the video manually as well and create any images you want if you don’t think the phone’s intelligence did a good job picking on its own.
Herein lies the real beauty of this system: you simply record the moment happening and decide later what you want to keep. There is no need to split your attention between capturing video of an event and taking photos, too. The only trade-off is that the initial video capture isn’t well stabilized and is lower resolution, although you can upload the file and have the Google servers boost the quality afterwards if you want.
![A pink petunia flower is highlighted with a white outline in a garden bed with other flowers and soil.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Moving-Object-800x450.jpg)
I’m really not a proponent of too much generative AI involved in my imagery, although some applications of the technology can be legitimately useful, and Magic Capture tends to land in that latter spot. I find it useful to have tools that will erase distractions of my choosing in the frame, but I’m not into changing skies or cutting objects and moving them around the frame.
I don’t want to generate new imagery or radically alter the subjects of my images, and Google has historically gone deep into the generative AI toolset, with the ability to upload images and have the servers wildly alter them.
This is why I was so surprised to see the Pixel 11 scale back this mindset somewhat with its latest phone.
![A great blue heron stands on rocks beside a small garden pond in a backyard.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/17866448487992-601x800.jpg)
Gone is the “Reimagine” function, which would let you access generative imagery with one button press. You will still find tools like the Magic Eraser and Move in the actions tab now, but any generative AI is now done via the Gemini assistant using Nano Banana, which is a separate interface. I tried this process to understand it and actually found it to be a frustrating experience. All the more reason to happily ignore it, and I’m glad it’s no longer a camera app function.
That doesn’t mean using Generative AI is gone, it’s just a more elongated process. You can still upload an image to Gemini, draw circles around areas and ask the software to add or change things, and you still get a relatively fake-looking result out of it. From there you have to download the finished image again, and send it into your photo gallery app. It’s a convoluted process, especially compared to last year’s setup, and — don’t get me wrong — I’m all for it being annoying. I’m just surprised Google is de-coupling AI from the experience to this degree after years of pushing it in our faces.
The result of this change is a deeper user experience in the camera app when it comes to actually making images. I like that I can choose to have quick controls for color filters and exposure changes right off the screen, or I can delve into the rather deep menus below my frame. I feel like the Pixel 11 Pro series provides plenty of customization and control of my images if I want to be more hands-on, but is still simple enough to be usable for casual users to enjoy. This shift in the control scheme and creative control is best exemplified with the new Looks color presets that are now available.
![A smartphone screen displays a photo editing interface with a black and white filter applied to an image of a leafy bush, showing adjustment sliders and a bottom menu with options for shadows, filters, sharpness, grain, and resetting.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Modifying-Looks-800x450.jpg)
The Looks tab brings up a series of color presets that apply any changes within the imaging pipeline. Rather than lay a color change on top of an existing image, these looks create the image as if it was taken that way in the first place. This allows for a meaningful amount of customization and color control within each preset. The premise is that image quality isn’t about always maximizing dynamic range or usable exposure, but is instead about achieving a feel or mood with our images that goes beyond numbers and values.
![A smartphone camera interface displays a view of yellow autumn leaves floating in a puddle reflecting trees, with manual white balance settings active.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Manual-Controls-800x450.jpg)
![A wooden post stands in calm water, surrounded by a small patch of grass and leaves, with tree reflections visible on the surface.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/PXL_20260813_193747797.RAW-01.COVER-LOOK-BLACK-TIE-ORANGE-FILTER-601x800.jpg)
The standard color mode has the option to deepen shadows or go with a softer color palette, and presets such as editorial or black tie tend to push the contrast higher. I like the Classic look with its warmer tones and controlled highlights, but some may prefer the Digi look with its lo-fi rendering and blown dynamic range.
What’s also important to understand is that each of these is simply a starting point that you can tweak, with full control of exposure, contrast, sharpness, white balance, tint, and more.
![](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/PXL_20260815_160046239.RAW-01.COVER-Classic-601x800.jpg)
You can make each of these looks work for you in a way that you enjoy, and I found this to be a refreshing change from the AI-everything approach that most phones use. The RAW files that you get will also save these changes baked in, so advanced users might still want to stick to a more generic approach and edit untouched RAW files in post, but most smartphone users want to discover their own way of rendering images and will appreciate the convenience of having the look fixed right out of the gate. You can also largely reverse the look of the DNG files that are produced, such as changing back to color in the Black Tie look or recovering lost highlights from the more dramatic looks.
![](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/PXL_20260815_160446617.RAW-01.COVER_-601x800.jpg)
![A sunset glows behind a line of trees along a riverbank, with three ducks swimming in the foreground water.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/PXL_20260818_023044169.RAW-01.COVER_-800x601.jpg)
Google Pixel 11 Pro XL Review: Video Features
The experience of shooting video on the Pixel 11 Pro is largely the same as last year, with a few new features. As before, it is capable of recording 4K video up to 60p, with the option to “Boost” the video to uncompressed 8K by uploading it to Google’s servers. There will of course be an improvement to footage shot with the telephoto camera due to the new larger sensor, but the process can take many hours to finalize.
![A smartphone screen displaying video settings, including options for flash, video boost, resolution, frame rate, and stabilization.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Active-Stabilizer-800x450.jpg)
The major new improvement to video quality comes from the new “Active Stabilization.” Similar to what Apple has offered for a few years, this mode switches to a wider camera and crops in to maximize digital stabilization. Oddly, it is only available in 1080p at 30p, with no support for 24p or 60p. This does certainly smooth out some bounce, but video quality also drops noticeably when using this feature.
![A smartphone camera interface displays a view of a paved path through a wooded area, with zoom controls, exposure settings, and a shutter button visible on the screen.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Horizontal-Interface-800x450.jpg)
The other major addition is the new “Creator” menu, which has several social media-targeted features. Most notable of these is the Teleprompter tool, which will display text on screen and automatically scroll at your talking speed. This works great, but obviously requires that you use the selfie camera to maintain access to the display, and that is the Pixel 11 Pro’s weakest camera. Beyond that, the text won’t flip for horizontal orientation, so you need to shoot in vertical mode to see your script properly. That feels like a particularly bizarre omission.
![A man wearing a baseball cap records a video outdoors, with a teleprompter overlay of text visible on the right side of the screen.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Teleprompter-800x450.jpg)
There is also a “Speech Enhancement” tool which applies digital filters to remove background noise. It works quite well, and doesn’t introduce a lot of digital artifacts into the soundtrack. We also have some small display features, like “Audio Visualizer,” which displays your audio levels, which is hardly a breakthrough technology, and “Social Media Grid”, which helps you frame for both 16:9 and 9:16. Bear in mind, though: using either of those frames will result in a substantial crop.
![A smartphone camera interface displays a view of a person riding a bicycle on a paved path through a wooded area.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Social-Media-Frame-800x450.jpg)
Google Pixel 11 Pro XL Review: Incremental Improvement
Many of this year’s improvements are incremental, which is what I’ve come to expect from smartphones and even full-size cameras in recent years. With a scant few exceptions, this has become the norm.
Most of the features that were introduced were pretty minor as well, although I can see how the Magic Capture function can be legitimately useful. It’s just a shame that the captured video has so many compromises.
Hardware changes are always positive and should be celebrated. The new telephoto camera is a much-needed improvement, and I liked the results. The new G6 Tensor processor also gave noticeably faster operation of image processing, and I really appreciated the lack of wait times to do high-res modes and Night Sight photography. Although low-light quality and portrait modes give very similar results to last year’s Pixel, the usable quality was already excellent, and the processing times are now far more convenient.
![A calm pond reflects a pastel sunset sky with pink and orange clouds, framed by grassy banks and silhouetted trees.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/PXL_20260815_025020467.NIGHT_.RAW-01.COVER_-800x601.jpg)
As far as the camera applications go, I was pleasantly impressed by the Pixel 11 Pro. I also appreciate the pull back on the AI-everything front, as minor as this change of direction might seem. The camera app feels more creative and less generative, and I support that move.
Unfortunately, the rising costs of memory and storage are going to hurt potential buyers here. Google is offering a 12GB of RAM version of the phone, which will be faster than last year’s phone by virtue of the improved processor, but the experience might not reflect that as the lower memory will slim the margins by which speed improves. To get a substantial improvement, you’ll need to go with the 16GB of RAM Pixel 11 Pro XL with 512GB of storage, and that starts at $1,419, and it goes up from there. As usual with smartphones across the board, I would only consider upgrading if you have a phone from at least a couple of generations back.
![A young girl in a baseball cap and Crocs fly fishes while standing on rocks in a river during a sunset.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/PXL_20260818_023620121.RAW-01.COVER_-800x601.jpg)
![Two weathered, metal utility boxes sit in a grassy area, with the smaller foreground box featuring a yellow "Caution: Buried Cable" sign and the larger background box displaying "Danger: High Voltage" warning labels.](https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/08/PXL_20260813_193158574.RAW-01.COVER-LOOKS-CLASSIC-601x800.jpg)
Are There Alternatives?
In North America, the main alternative will be the Samsung S26 Ultra, which will be a similar price for similar storage. I like the general camera capabilities, but Samsung is going hard and heavy towards integrated generative AI support within its camera app. If you want to play with AI, it is the more intuitive choice, but the Pixel feels more like a photographer’s phone. The Samsung S26 might also be a better video camera choice given its native 8K resolution and built-in support for log capture.
If you have access to other phone options and care about photography first and foremost, then I highly recommend the Xiaomi 17 Ultra.
Should You Buy It?
Yes, if only because North America has a limited number of high-end Android options that are easily available, and the Pixel feels like a more creative choice. If you are willing to bring in phones that your mobile carrier might not offer, you will find far more capable photographic options.
summary: The Google Pixel 11 Pro XL features minor external design updates, a new 6.8-inch screen reaching 3,600 nits, and a starting price of $1,299 due to industry-wide memory costs. Its primary hardware upgrade is a larger telephoto camera sensor delivering improved low-light performance and detail. Meanwhile, Google has shifted its generative AI features out of the main camera app and into a more convoluted process through the Gemini assistant.
key_points: The Pixel 11 Pro XL starts at $1,299 and features a 6.8-inch screen with a peak brightness of 3,600 nits.
The only major hardware upgrade is a new telephoto camera sensor providing a 5x zoom equivalent with better low-light quality and detail.
Battery capacity has dropped slightly to 5,115 mAh, though power efficiency from the G6 Tensor processor keeps longevity comparable to the previous model.
Magic Capture is a new video-based feature that extracts high-quality still images from recorded moments.
Generative AI tools like 'Reimagine' have been removed from the camera app and are now relegated to a more convoluted process via Gemini.

title: A week with the Pixel 11: 5 upgrades I already fell in love with
author: Rita El Khoury
content:
It's been a week since the Google Pixel 11 was announced, and a week since I've had my very own Pixel 11 in its recyclable box and cool Pistachio color.
This "baby Pixel" as I like to call it, or the base model, is the one I've been excited the most about this year. On paper, it takes everything that made the Pixel 10 so good in 2025 and makes it even better, with upgrades right where they matter the most.
In reality, I suspect it'll be the phone I recommend the most over the next 12 months because it provides the most value out of the entire lineup without breaking the bank, and while still offering some excellent features, like a zoom camera and the latest Tensor G6 processor.
But before I write my full review of the Pixel 11, which needs way more testing time than one week, I need to highlight a few changes that have already won me over.
256GB of storage is a great start
No one wants to worry about storage
I can already hear the counter-arguments raining: "I don't need 256GB of storage! Everything is in the cloud! I don't take photos or videos! Why should I pay more for a feature I won't use?"
Look, every phone out there, whether it costs $100 or $2,000, has something extra that you — personally — don't necessarily use, but the majority of buyers will need and use. 256GB of storage sits squarely in that category, in my opinion.
The Android system is already taking up 15GB of storage on my Pixel 11, and apps like Play Services, the Pixel Camera, and Google Search are already up to more than 1GB each. They will balloon further the more data they accumulate, and the more AI I use.
I've already used up 71GB of storage on this phone by just installing my apps, without moving any other data, and without taking more than a dozen photos and videos. If I ever plan to shoot some 4K video, I expect I'd be over 128GB in a couple of months. That's why starting out with 256GB of storage matters.
Better zoom, better portraits, better camera looks
This is the best "cheap flagship" camera setup
I don't know if we can call the Google Pixel 11 a "cheap flagship," but at $899, it certainly is one of the least expensive options among the more expensive flagship phones you can buy. And at that price, in the US, there isn't much competition with a decent 5x zoom camera.
Google has gone this year and improved it further. It can now go all the way up to 30x, and while that gives very questionable photos, the results are much nicer at 10x and 15x, which used to be a little less reliable last year on the Pixel 10.
On top of this, the Pixel 11 gets many of its Pro siblings' new camera features. I can shoot portraits at 5x now, instead of just 1x-2x. The new Magic Capture works decently well in my testing, but I'll report once I give it a proper run for its money over the weekend.
I'm also firmly in love with the new Camera Looks feature. I know it sounds like simple "filters" but I've found that the Vanilla look brings a bit of extra warmth to the photos — something Google's Pixels have been severely lacking over the last few years. And if I don't like it, I can tailor it to my preference.
The fact that I can change how pics look from the get-go, without having to dig into Google Photos and painstakingly edit them, one by one, is a huge time-saver and a big boon for someone like me who shoots 3,000+ pics a year and disliked the Pixel 10's flat colors.
The flatter camera bar is actually nice
I did not expect to like it this much
Google made a whole fuss about flattening the camera bar on its phones — it was even mentioned during the Made By Google livestream — but it's something that I chalked off as insignificant.
When I saw the Pixel 11 lineup in person, I went looking for that flat bar and didn't see it. It seemed to protrude just as much as on last year's models. Turns out this is only a change on the base Pixel 11, and not the Pro or Pro XL units, and I was looking in the wrong place.
And now that I've had the phone in my hand and inside a case, I can't believe I'm saying this, but I actually like it! The phone wobbles less on a table, especially when it vibrates. There's less risk of it sliding and gliding and falling on the floor. That's already a win.
Better yet, once I put Google's official case on, it fell nearly flush with the camera bar module, making the entire phone + case combo sit flat on my desk. Always. I shouldn't be happy about this — it makes no difference whatsoever to how I use my Pixel 11 — but I love it.
Faster wireless charging is also better
Qi2.2 with 25W makes a difference
Although the upgrade from 15W to 25W wireless charging doesn't seem too big on paper, it certainly makes a difference in my experience.
Last year, Qi2.2 didn't just make the Pixel 10 Pro XL charge slightly faster on wireless pads and power banks, it also caused less heat dissipation and kept the phone cooler during the process.
I've noticed this same effect on the Pixel 11 this year. With Qi2.2 25W and my Pixelsnap charger with Stand, or any of my Ugreen or Baseus chargers and power banks, the phone fills up decently fast and without getting too toasty. That's always a win for Pixels.
I like that bright display
My camera doesn't lie
Each time I've tried to take a photo of the Pixel 11, I've had to turn down the display's brightness to do that, because it is very bright. Up to 3,000 nits, and similar to my Pixel 11 Pro XL.
This isn't the kind of difference you will notice indoors or in dim environments, or in the foggy Parisian weather we've been having. But on a bright day, under the searing sun, like last Sunday, I was able to use the Pixel 11 without having to hold my hand over it to shade it and see what was on the display.
Google has also vastly raised the durability of its screens. There's a new Corning Glass Victus 2 glass on top of the display, which should be scratched less easily than the Pixel 11 series.
This will be a perfect upgrade from the Pixel 8 or 9
Look, no phone maker is angling its phones today as upgrades to last year's models. People wait two or three years between upgrades, and the Pixel 11 is likely to be the next phone for someone who has a Pixel 8 or 9. And for them, the changes will be huge.
An additional zoom camera, a much faster processor, a lot of AI smarts, a nicer and more durable design, a ton of new camera perks and features, fast wireless charging with built-in magnets for an entire ecosystem accessory, and on and on.
The Pixel 11 is a simple upgrade over last year's Pixel 10, but it fills in all the missing gaps and brings improvements in all the areas that matter. I can't wait to test it out more to have a more solid opinion about all the smart AI additions, too.

summary: After spending a week with the new Google Pixel 11, the reviewer highlights several standout upgrades that make the base model a compelling choice. Key improvements include a baseline of 256GB storage, enhanced camera capabilities with a 5x zoom and new Camera Looks, and a flatter camera bar design. Additional upgrades feature faster 25W wireless charging, a brighter display reaching up to 3,000 nits, and the Tensor G6 processor.
key_points: The Pixel 11 starts with 256GB of storage, accommodating heavy app usage, system data, and media.
Camera improvements include a better zoom up to 30x, 5x portrait shooting, and the new Camera Looks feature for instant style adjustments.
The redesigned flatter camera bar causes the phone to wobble less on flat surfaces and sit flush with official cases.

title: Rotherham patients say AI GP receptionist can't understand them
author: Lucy Ashton
content:
![A man and woman are sitting with their backs to the camera on a row of chairs in a GP reception area](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/b452/live/1ac08dc0-9a3f-11f1-ae41-df15e7357ff6.jpg)
New AI receptionists are causing problems for some patients in GP surgeries
- Published
Patients in Rotherham are struggling with a new artificial intelligence GP receptionist because it cannot understand the Yorkshire accent, according to a health watchdog.
Some surgeries are triaging patients using a nationwide AI system called EMMA to avoid long wait times on the phone.
Healthwatch Rotherham said some patients could not get the system to understand them as it does not respond well to variations in speech such as regional accents or speech impediments.
QuantumLoopAI, the company behind the system, said EMMA was designed to understand a range of dialects and patients can speak to a human at any time.
Healthwatch visited community groups to speak in particular to people who tend to be digitally excluded and might struggle with technology.
Manager Kym Gleeson said: "One of the issues is this system can't always understand what people's inquiry is about due to their broad Yorkshire accent.
"Across South Yorkshire, accents do vary quite a lot. There are different twangs so there's a lot of variation.
"It seems the system isn't always able to understand, so that causes frustration."
![A blurred image of a woman holding a mobile phone up in front of her face](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/2068/live/e27631d0-9a3f-11f1-ae41-df15e7357ff6.jpg)
Some patients are struggling on the telephone to GP surgeries
Healthwatch said its team had spoken in particular to elderly and veterans groups to inform them they can opt out of the system.
Gleeson said: "Practices use websites to triage but if you prefer to use the telephone it can be hard to navigate this AI system, especially if you're feeling quite vulnerable due to ill health.
"Some of the people said they had ended up going to the surgery in person because they felt using a telephone was no longer a comfortable process for them."
However, she said the EMMA system meant calls were navigated more swiftly.
"In that sense, it is a good system but for some people who don't want to tell AI their details, it is a concern," she added.
AI GP receptionist concerns in Rotherham
QuantumLoopAI said it understood patients' concerns and recognised there can be an adjustment period when new technology is introduced.
A spokesperson said: "EMMA does not make clinical decisions. She is designed and trained to understand a wide range of accents and dialects and supports 17 languages in addition to English.
"Where she is unable to understand or deal with a patient's request the call is transferred to the reception team. No caller is required to continue speaking with EMMA, and anyone can ask to speak to a member of staff at any time.
"EMMA is designed to improve access by answering calls instantly and removing telephone queues."
QuantumLoopAI added that feedback from practices and patients across the country has been "overwhelmingly positive" with more than 90% of patients reporting a positive improvement in service.
Legally, patients can ask for reasonable requirements to help them make an appointment and Healthwatch Rotherham said people should speak to practice managers.
It will pass its feedback to Healthwatch England, which will then report to the Department of Health and Social Care.
The NHS South Yorkshire Integrated Care Boards, which is responsible for local health service planning, said it was aware practices in South Yorkshire were using AI technology to manage reception services but was unable to say how many.
Anthony Fitzgerald, its executive lead for primary care, added: "We are currently working closely with Healthwatch colleagues to produce some guidance for practices on the use of AI telephone systems. This is an individual GP practice decision, within their contractual requirements."
summary: Patients in Rotherham are experiencing difficulties with a nationwide AI GP receptionist system called EMMA, which struggles to understand broad Yorkshire accents and regional speech variations. According to Healthwatch Rotherham, the technology has caused frustration and led some vulnerable or digitally excluded patients to visit surgeries in person instead. However, the system's developer, QuantumLoopAI, stated that EMMA is designed to handle various dialects, does not make clinical decisions, and allows callers to speak to a human staff member at any time.
key_points: Healthwatch Rotherham reports that the EMMA AI receptionist struggles to understand broad Yorkshire accents and speech impediments.
Some patients find navigating the phone system difficult when feeling vulnerable due to ill health, leading some to visit surgeries in person.
QuantumLoopAI stated that EMMA is designed to understand a wide range of dialects, supports 18 languages, and allows callers to transfer to a human at any time.
Healthwatch is informing groups about their right to opt out of the system and will pass feedback to Healthwatch England and the Department of Health and Social Care.

title: Special Porsche 911 GT3 commemorates 100 years of the Nürburgring | Evo
author: Ethan Jupp
content:
Special Porsche 911 GT3 commemorates 100 years of the Nürburgring
A new special edition from Porsche based on the GT3 wishes the Green Hell a happy hundredth birthday
![Porsche 911 GT3 100 Jahre Nürburgring](https://media.evo.co.uk/image/private/s--JDmDpsxf--/f_auto,t_content-image-mobile@1/v1787068136/evo/2026/08%20August/Porsche%20911%20GT3%20100%20Jahre%20Nu%CC%88rburgring%2001_hjg874.jpg)
In 2027 the Nürburgring turns 100 years old, so to commemorate such a momentous birthday, Porsche has created the 911 GT3 100 Jahre Nürburgring.
The car will come in either White or GT Silver Metallic, with a green wrap accent on the nose and rear trim in reference to the ‘Green Hell’ nickname for the ‘Ring coined by Sir Jackie Stewart. The car also gets green mirror caps and a green towing eye, with white arrows pointing to its location. There’s also a special historic Nürburgring logo on the wings and the choice of race numbers between 0 and 999, in a handwritten style, with bespoke B-pillar badges too. The wheels are California Gold.
Porsche will also make available a colour-coordinated version of the Manthey Racing kit for the GT3. It features green endplates featuring the ‘Ring’s outline and green and body colour wheel covers at the rear.
Open the door to this special GT3 and you’ll see the kick plates: Welcome to the Green Hell’ and projections of the circuit from the puddle lights. Better than ‘Icons of Cool’ I guess... The seats also feature green centres with the Nürburgring’s outline embroidered on the driver’s headrest. Manual or PDK is available, with the Walnut shifter of the Carrera T carrying over if the manual is chosen. Even the drive mode dial on the steering wheel features green highlights.
![Porsche 911 GT3 100 Jahre Nürburgring](https://media.evo.co.uk/image/private/s--ttUgc1Db--/f_auto,t_content-image-full-mobile@1/v1787068133/evo/2026/08%20August/Porsche%20911%20GT3%20100%20Jahre%20Nu%CC%88rburgring%2002_xif0m1.jpg)
If you can attribute the success of a car to its purpose and how fit for it it is, the Porsche likely owes a lot of the 911 GT3’s success to the popularity of the Nürburgring. If you’ve a certain amount of money to spend, there really is no better tool for the job of learning and dissecting the world’s most famous (and infamous) toll road. And everyone knows it, given there’s not a Tourist day or track day throughout the calendar year that doesn’t have at least a handful of the things in attendance.
It’s also the venue where 911s of all flavours, from the rally-ready Dakar to Porsche Motorsport’s GT3 R racers, are tested and honed to become the best they can be. A Porsche first took to the ‘Ring on 31 May 1953 – a 550 Spyder campaigned at the Eifelrennen. Porsche has won numerous races at the ‘Ring and has held numerous records. The overall record was held by a Porsche 956, driven by Stefan Bellof to 6:11.113 in 1983, for 35 years. Then in 2018, Porsche toppled itself, Timo Bernhard setting a 5:19.546 in the specially prepared Porsche 919 Hybrid Evo LMP1 car.
The ‘Ring is to the 911 and much of what Porsche does in general, what Ehra-Lessien is to a W16 Bugatti: nothing less than the most strenuous and arguably most important test for the car’s core principle. It’s right that Porsche should commemorate it. The question is, would you buy one of these GT3s?
summary: Porsche has created the 911 GT3 100 Jahre Nürburgring to commemorate the circuit's upcoming 100th birthday in 2027. The special edition features unique design elements referencing the "Green Hell" nickname, custom interior details, and an optional color-coordinated Manthey Racing kit. The model celebrates the deep history and testing relationship between Porsche and the famous German racetrack.
key_points: Porsche announced the 911 GT3 100 Jahre Nürburgring to celebrate the Nürburgring's centenary in 2027.
The car includes exterior styling cues such as White or GT Silver Metallic paint, green wrap accents, California Gold wheels, and historic Nürburgring logos.
Interior features include custom kick plates, puddle light circuit projections, embroidered headrests, and green highlights.
A colour-coordinated Manthey Racing kit is also available for the GT3 edition.
Porsche has a long-standing testing and racing history at the Nürburgring dating back to 1953.

title: Pixel 11 Pro's telephoto camera has an upgrade Google forgot to mention
author: Taylor Kerns
content:
Pixel 11 Pro's telephoto camera has an upgrade Google forgot to mention
Aug 19, 2026 — 10:22 AM ET
![google pixel 11 pro vs pixel 10 pro hands on 3 Google Pixel 11 Pro next to Pixel 10 Pro.](https://www.androidauthority.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/google-pixel-11-pro-vs-pixel-10-pro-hands-on-3-scaled.jpg)
- The Pixel 11 Pro comes with an upgraded telephoto camera sensor.
- As demonstrated by a Reddit user, compared to the Pixel 10 Pro and 9 Pro, the Pixel 11 Pro’s telephoto camera can focus on closer subjects.
- Google hasn’t responded to our request for comment.
The Pixel 11 Pro comes with quite a few low-key upgrades, including a new telephoto camera sensor. The new sensor is the same 48-megapixel resolution as the one used in the Pixel 10 Pro and 9 Pro, but the 11 Pro’s version is a little larger compared to the one used in the previous to generations. That should make for better low-light performance, but the upgraded telephoto hardware also brings another, smaller improvement: it can focus on closer subjects.
As shared by user pcman2000 on Reddit early this morning, the Pixel 11 Pro’s telephoto camera is apparently able to focus much closer to the phone than the telephoto in the Pixel 9 Pro. They shared an image showing their Pixel 11 Pro next to a 9 Pro, both with their camera apps in manual mode and their telephoto cameras’ focus sliders set to the minimum distance. The 11 Pro is sharply focused on its box situated a couple of feet away, while the 9 Pro’s image is very blurry.
![pixel 11 pro v 9 pro telephoto focus pixel 11 pro v 9 pro telephoto focus](https://www.androidauthority.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/pixel-11-pro-v-9-pro-telephoto-focus.jpeg)
Both the Pixel 9 Pro and the Pixel 10 Pro feature Sony’s IMX858 sensor in their telephoto cameras, a 48-megapixel, 1/2.55″ model. The 11 Pro, meanwhile, uses a 48-megapixel, 1/1.95″ sensor that, as far as I know, hasn’t been publicly identified yet.
The option to focus on closer subjects using a telephoto camera might not seem all that important, but that flexibility makes for more options when framing a shot, which is always a plus.
We don’t have official info about either camera’s minimum focus distance, but pcman2000 says the 11 Pro’s seems like “about half (or maybe even slightly less) the distance of my Pixel 9 Pro’s 5x camera.” Google didn’t make this upgrade part of its pitch for the Pixel 11 Pro, but a win’s a win. As of publication, Google hasn’t responded to Android Authority‘s request for more info.
summary: The Google Pixel 11 Pro features an unannounced upgrade to its telephoto camera sensor, improving both low-light performance and the ability to focus on closer subjects. While it retains the 48-megapixel resolution of previous generations, the new sensor is physically larger. This enhancement provides users with greater framing flexibility, allowing the telephoto lens to focus at a significantly shorter minimum distance than the Pixel 9 Pro and Pixel 10 Pro.
key_points: The Pixel 11 Pro includes a larger 48-megapixel telephoto camera sensor compared to the Pixel 9 Pro and 10 Pro.
The upgraded hardware allows the telephoto camera to focus on much closer subjects.
A Reddit user demonstrated that the 11 Pro can sharply focus at a fraction of the minimum distance required by older models.
Google did not mention this telephoto upgrade in its official product pitch and has not responded to requests for comment.

As we can see, it’s a fairly flat $100/£80 increase across the board. It also unfortunately means that the cheapest model in the line-up — the standard Pixel 11 — has seen the highest percentage price increase.
Price hikes are never good, but with the Pixel 11, it feels particularly damning.
Google Pixel 11 series: Hot or Not?
No price hike is good — but this one’s especially bad
I’ve long maintained that if I were to leave the consumer tech journalism business, and therefore had to buy my own phones again, I’d start with a Pro Pixel. Not just because Pixel phones are good to use and full of interesting features, but because they’ve been cheaper than the competition.
This feeling came about when the Pixel 6 series arrived in 2021. Like a lot of people, this was the moment when Google’s Pixel phones went from an also-ran in my mind to a Samsung/Apple-level big player in the smartphone hardware world. While the Pixel doesn’t account for as much of annual smartphone sales as those other two companies, I’ve started to see normal people buying and enjoying these phones, rather than them being wielded exclusively by my gadget-geek peers.
Over time, the price difference has shrunk, and my certainty has wavered.
I think a large factor in the sudden rise of the Pixel was its price. Going back to the Pixel 6, it cost $599/£599 for the standard model and $ 899/£849 for the Pro (which is equivalent in size and features to the current Pro XL model). At the same time, Apple’s iPhone 13 and Samsung’s Galaxy S22 cost $799, while the iPhone 13 Pro Max and Galaxy S22 Ultra cost $1,099 and $1,199, respectively.
![google pixel 11 vs samsung galaxy s26 Photos of the Google Pixel 11 and Samsung Galaxy S26 next to each other.](https://www.androidauthority.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/google-pixel-11-vs-samsung-galaxy-s26-scaled.jpg)
But over time, the price difference has shrunk, and my certainty has wavered. As we see above, the Pixel 10 series matched the prices that Apple and Samsung had been offering their phones at for several years. Fortunately for Google, the Pixel 10 managed to get a few months as a “budget” pick again due to the price hike given to the Galaxy S26 series earlier this year.
But now Samsung and Google are on an even playing field again, and you’ll pay at least $899 whether you choose the Galaxy S26 or Pixel 11. And somehow, it’s Apple that’s selling the cheapest flagship phone of the big three phone makers in the West, with the iPhone 17 retailing for $799.
Take away the price advantage in a year where Google hasn’t made significant battery, performance, or camera changes with the Pixel 11, and you start to wonder what the point of the Pixel is at this point.
It both is and isn’t Google’s fault
![google pixel 11 pro series all colors The Google Pixel 11 Pro phones in all four colors.](https://www.androidauthority.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/google-pixel-11-pro-series-all-colors-scaled.jpg)
We are unfortunately living at a time when tech is becoming more expensive, with much of that due to RAM shortages that are hiking the prices of basic phone components. And since that’s almost exclusively because of the genAI boom, Google — as one of the biggest players in the sector — bears a fair amount of responsibility for this self-inflicted wound.
I still feel that Google could have swallowed more of the component cost to protect the Pixel 11 series from price hikes.
But I don’t feel sorry for Google; I feel sorry for smartphone buyers. Users who are intrigued by the new HiLight feature, have to pay more for the privilege. Meanwhile, users who just want a good deal on a flagship-grade device now have even more limited options. And in a smartphone market that keeps losing competitors as participating brands stop selling in certain countries or give up on phones altogether, Google’s decision ends up having an outsized impact.
Even if manufacturing costs are higher, I still feel that Google could have absorbed more of the component costs to protect the Pixel 11 series from price hikes. Google is always prompting us to “ask more of your phone” in its advertising. I feel keeping the price down isn’t an unreasonable request.
![Google Pixel 11](https://clearbuy-cloud.nyc3.digitaloceanspaces.com/media/12549/custom_filename.jpg)
![Google Pixel 11 Pro](https://clearbuy-cloud.nyc3.digitaloceanspaces.com/media/12553/custom_filename.jpg)
![Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold](https://clearbuy-cloud.nyc3.digitaloceanspaces.com/media/12561/custom_filename.jpg)
summary: The Google Pixel 11 series launched with universal price increases of $100 or £80 across all four models. This hike eliminates the traditional price advantage that made Pixel phones a compelling recommendation compared to competitors like Apple and Samsung. Rising component costs driven by the generative AI boom contributed to the price increases, leaving consumers with fewer budget-friendly flagship options.
key_points: The Google Pixel 11 series features a flat $100/£80 price increase across its lineup.
The standard Pixel 11 now costs $899, matching the price of competing devices like the Samsung Galaxy S26.
Apple currently sells the cheapest flagship phone among the major Western brands with the $799 iPhone 17.
Rising component costs related to the generative AI boom have contributed to higher tech prices.
The author argues that Google should have absorbed more of the component costs to protect consumers from the price hikes.

title: ‘GTA VI’ Leaker Drops Even More New Footage, Reveals Motivations
author: Paul Tassi
content:
Last night, Rockstar was plagued by yet another leak of Grand Theft Auto VI footage, this time just a few months ahead of the game’s release in November. The leaker, known as Cyberleek, has released footage of gameplay and the map of GTA VI, content that Take-Two has been issuing takedowns for since its release, though the social media spread is largely uncontained.
Cyberleek has been vocal about the leak and has actually spelled out their motivations for doing it. In a statement, they said: “A digital copy cannot sell out. Yet publishers kept the preorder system and stripped away its only consumer benefit. Now gamers pay early and receive nothing in return except a countdown timer and a cosmetic skin."
This is in the wake of Take-Two announcing there would be no physical copies of GTA VI for consoles. Purchasing a box copy would contain nothing more than a code. The move is adjacent to Sony announcing it would produce no more physical games in 2028, but Rockstar’s move starts this year, which will net it a better return on its $80 game, on that will sell tens of millions of copies.
There may be alternative motivations here, as many of the releases contain watermarks promoting a specific cryptocurrency for purchase, suggesting the leaker is trying to get something out of this besides internet infamy.
